title: Semantic HTML
subtitle: Header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer and semantic document structure.
description: Write cleaner, more meaningful HTML that improves accessibility and maintainability.

blocks.text: Welcome to Lesson 7: Semantic HTML. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “Semantic HTML”. The goal is to header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer and semantic document structure.. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.

Semantic elements communicate the purpose of page regions. A header introduces a page or section, nav contains important navigation, main identifies the central content, and footer holds related closing information.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select HTML. Paste this snippet into the matching web/React editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.question: A document has repeated navigation, a main learning area, and a footer. Which design communicates those regions most clearly?
options: A single paragraph with manual spaces.
Only nested span elements.
A table for every region.
Use header/nav/main/footer elements where their meanings fit.
blocks.explanation: Landmark elements make page regions easier to understand and navigate.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Landmark elements make page regions easier to understand and navigate.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Landmark elements make page regions easier to understand and navigate.

blocks.text: PAGE 2 — Build the idea step by step

The dashboard frames the practical purpose this way: “Write cleaner, more meaningful HTML that improves accessibility and maintainability.” Use the examples as small experiments, not as code to memorize. A strong result is one you can explain and then adapt to a slightly different requirement.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select HTML. Paste this snippet into the matching web/React editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

Application tip: in a real HTML project, choose names and structures that reveal the reason the code exists. Do not copy a snippet into a project without checking its assumptions and adapting it to the surrounding code.

blocks.explanation: The main landmark identifies the page’s dominant content.

blocks.text: Use section when a thematic grouping needs its own heading and article for a self-contained piece of content. Do not replace every div automatically; choose semantic elements when their meaning fits.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select HTML. Paste this snippet into the matching web/React editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.question: When is article a sensible choice?
options: For every single word.
For a self-contained item such as an independent post or lesson note.
Only for layout spacing.
Whenever a border is required.
blocks.explanation: Article is intended for self-contained content that can make sense as an independent item.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Article is intended for self-contained content that can make sense as an independent item.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Article is intended for self-contained content that can make sense as an independent item.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Apply it and check your reasoning

Semantic structure helps other developers, browser tools, and assistive technology understand the page. It does not automatically guarantee accessibility, so headings, labels, contrast, and keyboard behavior still need attention.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select HTML. Paste this snippet into the matching web/React editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

Before continuing, explain in your own words how this topic helps solve the dashboard goal: Write cleaner, more meaningful HTML that improves accessibility and maintainability. Try one boundary case, one normal case, and one case that should be rejected or handled differently.

blocks.question: A HTML program runs on a teammate’s device but fails on yours. What is the best first debugging step?
options: Rewrite the entire program in another language.
Compare the runtime/compiler, run instructions, and first error message.
Delete the imports and hope it runs.
Change several unrelated lines at once.
blocks.explanation: Environment differences and the first reported error are the most useful starting evidence. Change one thing at a time so the cause remains clear.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Environment differences and the first reported error are the most useful starting evidence. Change one thing at a time so the cause remains clear.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Environment differences and the first reported error are the most useful starting evidence. Change one thing at a time so the cause remains clear.

blocks.question: A new project needs to be maintained by another developer. Which choice helps most?
options: Use a clear entry point, meaningful names, and documented run steps.
Put every instruction on one line.
Use unexplained abbreviations for every name.
Avoid testing because the project is small.
blocks.explanation: Clear structure and reproducible run steps help another developer understand and verify the program.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Clear structure and reproducible run steps help another developer understand and verify the program.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Clear structure and reproducible run steps help another developer understand and verify the program.
